turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Aoife Brennan? In you come. I'll do the checks before Dr Walsh sees you. Coat on the chair is grand.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Thanks. The traffic out of Salthill was desperate, we were stuck at the roundabout, and your man in the white van wouldn't budge.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's grand, we weren't that late. I'm Declan, her husband. I came in with her.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): No bother. Blood pressure is 128 over 78, pulse is 74, temperature 36.6. All fine. He'll be along in a minute.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): 36.6. I always think that's the weather. It was lashing on the prom this morning, waves up over the wall.
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): That's a normal temperature. I'll leave ye to it.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello Aoife, Declan. Dr Walsh. Have a seat. What has ye in?

[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's not herself since she lost the job. She's not sleeping, she's no energy, and she's lost interest in near everything. I've been on at her for months to come in.

[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm fine. Honestly, he's making a mountain of it. We were only talking about the neighbour's extension, the blocks came on a Tuesday and they're still in a heap. Gas, isn't it?
[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll park the blocks. Declan, the sleep — what are you actually seeing at home?
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Awake half the night. I'd put it at about three months, since around March, when the redundancy really hit.

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Three months? Ah no, it's longer than that. Six months, maybe eight. It started after I was let go from the credit union. When was that... last winter, or the one before? I couldn't put a date on it if you paid me.

[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to invent a start date. Declan has three months, you have six or eight and a winter you can't place. Roughly three to eight months, and the date stays unclear. Aoife, how is the night for you, in your own words?

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Well. If I'm honest the sleep is desperate. I drop off grand and then I'm awake at three, staring at the ceiling, and the next day is a write-off. So he's not entirely wrong.
[SEG0015] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And the energy is gone. She used to be up and out. Now it's the couch.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): The couch is lovely though. We got it in Harvey Norman, the green one, and Barney — the dog, a terrier mix — thinks he owns it. Mad as a brush.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Fair play to Barney. The energy, Aoife. Are you wrecked, or is Declan laying it on?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm wrecked, yeah. Low energy, most days. Now that I'm here I won't pretend. Even making the tea feels like a job of work.
[SEG0019] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And no interest in anything. Not the GAA, not the friends, not the baking.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm fine with the baking, I did scones on Sunday, raisin ones. But the matches, yeah, I don't fancy them anymore. I still walk Barney. So it's not everything, Declan.

[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Interest is down in things you liked, not wiped out. I'm wondering already if the redundancy knocked the mood, with the sleep and the energy in the same picture. Can you tell me about the job?

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): They let a load of us go. Your man the manager was sorry, in fairness, nearly crying himself. I liked the counter, the bit of craic with the regulars. Now the days just stretch.
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And she's hardly eating, doctor. I put the dinner down and it comes back barely touched.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): That is not true. I'm eating grand. I had a fry this morning, rashers and pudding. Don't be telling him I'm wasting away.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): So ye're not agreed. Declan, you see a loss of appetite. Aoife, you're saying the eating is fine. I won't pick a winner, I'll just hold both.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. The fry was from the caff on the prom, not even homemade, which is lazy of me. The pudding was lovely though.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): How is the mood itself? Flat, sad, snappy?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Flat. That's the word. Not sobbing-in-Tesco flat, though I did get weepy at an ad for paint, which is ridiculous. Mostly I can't be bothered.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): I have to ask this gently, and you can answer straight. Have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself, or that you'd be better off not here?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No. God, no. I've never had thoughts of harming myself. Not once. I want to be here for Barney and for himself, I'm just stuck.
[SEG0031] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's said nothing like that at home either.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good, and I'm glad that's clear. If it ever changed, you wouldn't sit on it — same day, ring us or go to the emergency department. Alright?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I would. I'm not that kind of stuck. My aunt used to say mind yourself like it was a full sentence.
[SEG0034] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Her mother went through a long depression after Aoife's father died. She was on a tablet for the mood. I never knew the name of it.

[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Mam was, yeah, for years. And my sister Orla is obsessed with biotin for the hair, she gets it in the chemist, but that's Orla's, I don't take it. A bit of grey never killed anyone.
[SEG0036] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm on metformin myself, five hundred milligrams twice a day, for the diabetes. Just so that's not mixed up. Aoife isn't on it.

[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good you said it. The metformin is yours, Declan, and the biotin is Orla's. Neither goes on Aoife's chart. Mother's depression I'll note in the family history. Aoife, any medicine of your own?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Only vitamin D from the chemist. A thousand units, the little capsule. I'm meant to take it every day.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Meant to. More often than not it's sitting in the press. I wouldn't say she takes it the way it says on the tub.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah, Declan. I take it. Well, some days. Um, I actually don't know how often, now that you ask. Most weeks I miss a few.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): So vitamin D, a thousand units, meant to be daily, and whether it gets taken is up in the air. Anything you've stopped?

[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): No regular ones. I had the gallbladder out, three years ago in the summer, and they said no tablets after. The surgeon was a lovely fella from Cork, talked hurling the whole time.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): Grand. I'm not marching through every system, and I won't quiz you on allergies or smoking or the drink. None of that is why ye're here. Let me think out loud.

[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): Broken sleep, flat mood, low energy, less interest, all after the redundancy, running roughly three to eight months with no firm date. Appetite is disputed between ye. No thoughts of self-harm. My working impression is a depressive episode after the job loss, but it could just as easily be an adjustment to being let go. I can't separate those today, so both stay open.

[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Adjustment sounds nicer. Like I'll adjust and then I'll be flying. There was a library job and I didn't even open the link. Then I watched half of Fair City and fell asleep on the dog.

[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): That fits the interest piece. A tablet such as sertraline can help this picture, and fifty milligrams is the usual place to start. But I am not starting it today. If the sleep and the mood haven't lifted by the time I see you again, then we can look at starting the sertraline.
[SEG0047] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Would a sleeping tablet not be quicker? She bought a herbal thing once.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): That was valerian, from the health shop. I took it twice and it was useless, so I stopped. Tasted like old socks. I wouldn't go back to it.

[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): Leaving the valerian stopped is right, it rarely does much. Sertraline stays a maybe, not a script today. I don't want bloods for the sake of it. If you're no better at the review, then we can do a thyroid blood test. Not today.

[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): My friend Nuala had the thyroid out and she's on thyroxine, Eltroxin she calls it. That's Nuala in Oranmore, not me. Her roses are the size of your fist, I don't know how, the wind would skin you.

[SEG0051] person_4 (DOCTOR): Nuala's Eltroxin stays with Nuala. For you, the useful things are plain. Same bedtime and same getting-up time, the dog walk in daylight, and ease off the tea after the afternoon. That's for you to try, not a prescription.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): The tea will be the hard part. Barry's, two sugars, Declan says it's a crime. I'll try the daylight walk. Barney will think it's Christmas.
[SEG0053] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll walk with her if she'll have me. And I'll try to stop answering for her.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): You do answer for me, but you mean well. The scones were raisin, did I say? My mother put a pinch of salt in the flour. That's the trick.

[SEG0055] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back here in a month, either way, not only if you're worse. I want that visit. And if you feel unsafe before then, don't wait, come in or go to the emergency department.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): A month is grand. Will the parking still be a nightmare? We drove around for twenty minutes. There's a spot by the church if you're bold enough.
[SEG0057] person_4 (DOCTOR): Parking I can't fix. Reception will send the appointment. Anything we didn't touch that you wanted in?
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't think so. The credit union sent a spa voucher and I laughed, because a facial won't fix the three-in-the-morning ceiling. Decent of them, though.
[SEG0059] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She has the radio on at night when she can't sleep. Newstalk. I don't think it helps.
[SEG0060] person_4 (DOCTOR): The news at that hour can wind you up. If you're awake, leave the radio off. Dim light, no Newstalk. Same sort of advice as the tea.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, the news does my head in then. I'll leave it off. Declan hogs the good pillow anyway, that's a separate row.
[SEG0062] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The pillow is mine, for the record. Do we need a sick note? She's not working.
[SEG0063] person_4 (DOCTOR): No sick note while she's not in work. If she starts somewhere and needs one, we can do it then. Not today.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): I might do the library thing. Or I might not. Sorry for rabbitting, I do that when I'm nervous. The magazines out there are from 2019, I'd say.

[SEG0065] person_4 (DOCTOR): Rabbit away, it's useful. So, to land it: no new tablet today, sertraline only if you're no better next time, thyroid bloods only in that same case, the sleep habits are yours to try, and I'll see you in a month. If you feel in danger, you don't wait.
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand. Thanks, doctor. Come on, Declan, before Barney eats the couch.
